quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on how contribution and break-even are set up for a spinning mill, a weaving shed and a dyeing plant.

questions.q: In the spinning mill sheet, contribution per lb is
options: Yarn price per lb − net cost of raw material per lb
Yarn price per lb − daily fixed cost per lb
Net cost of raw material per lb − yarn price per lb
Yarn price per lb ÷ bags per day
questions.explain: Contribution is price minus the variable cost, and in the simplified sheet the only variable cost is the net raw material: Rs 51 − Rs 35 = Rs 16 per lb.

questions.q: A 'bag' of yarn in the spinning example weighs
questions.explain: The sheet states daily production in bags of 100 lb; the yarn price is quoted per 10 lb (Rs 510), which is a different unit.

questions.q: Which of these appears in the monthly fixed cost of all three plants?
questions.explain: Depreciation, financial charges, administration and miscellaneous make up the fixed cost in every sheet; cotton, yarn and dyes are the variable material costs.

questions.q: The daily fixed cost in each sheet is found by dividing the monthly fixed cost by 30.
questions.explain: The spinning sheet labels the row 'Daily fixed cost (÷30)': Rs 11,400,000 ÷ 30 = Rs 380,000, and the other plants follow the same rule.

questions.q: 'Commission finishing' in the dyeing example means the plant
options: Buys grey fabric, dyes it and sells it
Processes customers' fabric for a charge per metre
questions.explain: A commission dyer does not own the fabric; it earns charges per metre and its variable costs are dyes, chemicals, utilities and miscellaneous.

questions.q: In the weaving sheet, 20×16/128×60 63″ describes
options: The fabric construction: warp and weft counts, ends and picks per inch, and width
The number of looms and shifts
questions.explain: Warp Ne 20, weft Ne 16, 128 ends and 60 picks per inch, 63 inches wide — the quality running on the 120 air-jet looms.

questions.q: Break-even for the weaving shed is expressed per loom per day because
options: Fixed cost is divided equally among the looms
questions.explain: Daily fixed cost Rs 480,000 ÷ 120 looms = Rs 4,000 per loom, so the break-even question becomes how many metres each loom must weave to earn Rs 4,000 of contribution.

questions.q: Fixed cost per metre in the dyeing sheet (Rs 9.60) is
options: Charges per metre − contribution per metre
Contribution per metre − profit per metre
questions.explain: Rs 480,000 ÷ 50,000 m = Rs 9.60; it is valid only at that volume, which is exactly why break-even is computed separately.

questions.q: In the dyeing sheet the contribution per metre is the charge per metre minus the cost of dyes, chemicals, utilities and miscellaneous per metre.
questions.explain: The variable costs listed are dyes and chemicals, and utilities and miscellaneous per metre; the Rs 12 contribution is what remains of the charge after these.

questions.q: The lecture's closing remark describes the weaving margin as
options: Comfortable, because looms run three shifts
Thin — one rupee per metre on yarn price removes the whole profit
questions.explain: Contribution of Rs 9 falling to Rs 8 gives 8 × 500 m = Rs 4,000 per loom per day, exactly the fixed cost per loom, so profit disappears.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The formulas behind the three sheets, and which way each figure moves when an input changes.

questions.q: Daily contribution of the spinning mill is
options: Contribution per lb × bags per day
Contribution per lb × bags per day × 100
Yarn price per lb × bags per day × 100
questions.explain: Each bag is 100 lb, so Rs 16 × 250 × 100 = Rs 400,000. Forgetting the 100 lb per bag gives Rs 4,000 — a thousandfold error.

questions.q: Break-even bags per day for the spinning mill equals
options: Daily fixed cost ÷ contribution per lb
Monthly fixed cost ÷ contribution per lb
questions.explain: Rs 380,000 ÷ (16 × 100) = 237.5 bags. Dividing by the per-lb contribution gives lb, not bags.

questions.q: If the yarn price rises from Rs 510 to Rs 520 per 10 lb with cotton unchanged, the contribution per lb becomes
questions.explain: Rs 520 per 10 lb is Rs 52 per lb; 52 − 35 = Rs 17. Rs 26 wrongly adds Rs 10 instead of Rs 1 per lb.

questions.q: Break-even metres per loom per day in the weaving shed is
options: Daily fixed cost per loom ÷ contribution per metre
Daily fixed cost ÷ contribution per metre
Contribution per metre ÷ daily fixed cost per loom
Daily production per loom ÷ contribution per metre
questions.explain: Rs 4,000 ÷ Rs 9 = 444.4 m per loom per day. Using the whole shed's fixed cost would give the shed's break-even metres (53,333 m), not the per-loom figure.

questions.q: If the monthly fixed cost of the dyeing plant rises, its break-even metres per day rise in proportion.
questions.explain: Break-even = daily fixed cost ÷ contribution per metre, so with contribution unchanged the break-even volume is proportional to the fixed cost.

questions.q: Monthly profit in each sheet is found as
questions.explain: Rs 20,000 × 30 = Rs 600,000 for spinning and Rs 60,000 × 30 = Rs 1,800,000 for weaving; the sheets assume 30 working days, consistent with dividing monthly fixed cost by 30.

questions.q: If the dyeing plant's output rises from 50,000 m to 60,000 m a day, the fixed cost per metre
questions.explain: Rs 480,000 ÷ 60,000 = Rs 8.00; the total fixed cost is unchanged, so spreading it over more metres lowers the per-metre figure.

questions.q: Which change would raise the weaving shed's break-even metres per loom?
options: A lower cost of yarn per metre
A higher cost of yarn per metre
questions.explain: Higher yarn cost lowers the Rs 9 contribution, the denominator of fixed cost ÷ contribution, so more metres are needed. The other three changes all lower the break-even.

questions.q: The daily profit of the weaving shed equals profit per loom per day multiplied by the number of looms.
questions.explain: Rs 500 per loom × 120 looms = Rs 60,000 per day, as the sheet shows.

questions.q: Profit per day in the spinning sheet is
options: Yarn price × production − monthly fixed cost
questions.explain: Rs 400,000 − Rs 380,000 = Rs 20,000 per day. Using the monthly fixed cost against a daily contribution is a common unit mix-up.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Recompute the three sheets and try a few what-if figures for each plant.

questions.q: Yarn sells at Rs 510 per 10 lb and the net cost of raw material is Rs 35 per lb. What is the contribution per lb?
questions.explain: Price per lb = 510 ÷ 10 = Rs 51; contribution = 51 − 35 = Rs 16 per lb.

questions.q: A spinning mill produces 250 bags of 100 lb a day with contribution Rs 16 per lb. What is the daily contribution?
Monthly fixed cost of the spinning mill is Rs 11,400,000 and contribution is Rs 16 per lb. How many bags of 100 lb per day are needed to break even (30-day month)?
questions.explain: Daily fixed cost = 11,400,000 ÷ 30 = Rs 380,000; ÷ (16 × 100) = 237.5 bags per day.

questions.q: A weaving shed of 120 looms has monthly fixed cost Rs 14,400,000. What is the daily fixed cost per loom (30-day month)?
Daily fixed cost per loom is Rs 4,000 and contribution is Rs 9 per metre. Break-even metres per loom per day, to one decimal?
questions.explain: 4,000 ÷ 9 = 444.4 m per loom per day.

questions.q: A loom weaves 500 m a day at Rs 9 contribution per metre and carries Rs 4,000 of daily fixed cost. What is the profit per loom per day?
questions.explain: Contribution = 500 × 9 = Rs 4,500; profit = 4,500 − 4,000 = Rs 500 per loom per day.

questions.q: The dyeing plant's monthly fixed cost is depreciation 5.6 M + financial charges 6.5 M + administration 0.3 M + miscellaneous 2.0 M. Its daily fixed cost (30 days) is?
questions.explain: Monthly total = Rs 14,400,000; ÷ 30 = Rs 480,000 per day.

questions.q: The dyeing plant processes 50,000 m a day with contribution Rs 12 per metre and daily fixed cost Rs 480,000. Monthly profit (30 days)?
The dyeing plant's break-even metres per day with daily fixed cost Rs 480,000 and contribution Rs 12 per metre is
questions.explain: 480,000 ÷ 12 = 40,000 m. 50,000 m is the actual production, and 57,600 comes from multiplying rather than dividing.

questions.q: If the spinning mill's yarn price falls to Rs 500 per 10 lb (cotton still Rs 35 per lb), the daily profit at 250 bags becomes
questions.explain: Contribution = 50 − 35 = Rs 15; daily contribution = 15 × 25,000 = 375,000; 375,000 − 380,000 = −Rs 5,000. A Rs 1 per lb price drop costs Rs 25,000 a day.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Mill decisions where the three sheets tell you what will happen to profit.

questions.q: The weaving shed's yarn supplier raises the price so that yarn and materials cost Rs 1 more per metre. With 500 m per loom and Rs 4,000 fixed cost per loom, the shed
options: Still earns Rs 500 per loom per day
Loses Rs 500 per loom per day
Earns Rs 4,000 per loom per day
questions.explain: Contribution drops from Rs 9 to Rs 8; 8 × 500 = Rs 4,000 = the daily fixed cost per loom, so profit is zero — the lecture's own warning.

questions.q: A buyer offers the dyeing plant 10,000 m a day extra at a charge Rs 3 per metre below the normal rate (normal contribution Rs 12). Capacity is available. The plant should
options: Refuse — the price is below the usual charge
Accept — each metre still adds Rs 9 contribution with fixed cost unchanged
Accept only if fixed cost per metre falls below Rs 3
Refuse — profit per metre becomes negative
questions.explain: With spare capacity fixed cost does not change, so any positive contribution (12 − 3 = Rs 9 per metre, Rs 90,000 a day) adds to profit.

questions.q: The spinning mill is running at 240 bags a day. The sales office asks whether the mill is profitable. Your answer is
options: Yes, because 240 is above break-even of 237.5
No, because fixed cost per bag is too high
questions.explain: Break-even is 237.5 bags; at 240 bags the mill earns (240 − 237.5) × 1,600 = Rs 4,000 a day. Positive contribution alone does not guarantee profit.

questions.q: Ten of the 120 looms are stopped for a month for overhaul. The others still weave 500 m each at Rs 9 contribution; the shed's daily fixed cost remains Rs 480,000. What is the new daily profit (or loss, as a negative number)?
questions.explain: Contribution = 110 × 500 × 9 = Rs 495,000; profit = 495,000 − 480,000 = Rs 15,000 a day, down from Rs 60,000 because the idle looms' Rs 40,000 of fixed cost is still paid.

questions.q: If the weaving shed buys ten more looms, the lecture's break-even of 444.4 m per loom per day will certainly stay the same.
questions.explain: More looms raise depreciation and financial charges, so the daily fixed cost per loom may change; break-even per loom must be recalculated with the new fixed cost.

questions.q: A dyeing manager wants to reduce the break-even point. Which action does NOT help?
options: Reducing financial charges by repaying a loan
Increasing daily production from 50,000 to 55,000 m
questions.explain: Break-even = fixed cost ÷ contribution per metre; more production raises profit but leaves the break-even volume itself unchanged.

questions.q: Cotton prices rise so that the net raw material cost becomes Rs 38 per lb while yarn stays at Rs 51 per lb. At 250 bags a day the spinning mill now
questions.explain: Contribution = 51 − 38 = Rs 13; 13 × 25,000 = 325,000; 325,000 − 380,000 = −Rs 55,000 per day. Rs 325,000 is the contribution, not the profit.

questions.q: To compare the three plants' robustness, which figure best shows how far each is above break-even?
questions.explain: Spinning 250 ÷ 237.5 = 1.05, weaving 500 ÷ 444.4 = 1.13, dyeing 50,000 ÷ 40,000 = 1.25 — the dyeing plant has the most cushion, spinning the least.

questions.q: The spinning mill wants a monthly profit of Rs 1,500,000 instead of Rs 600,000. With contribution Rs 1,600 per bag and daily fixed cost Rs 380,000, how many bags per day must it make (30 days)? Give one decimal.
The weaving manager proposes a faster weft insertion that lifts output to 550 m per loom per day with no change in fixed cost or contribution. Profit per loom per day becomes
questions.explain: 550 × 9 = 4,950 contribution; 4,950 − 4,000 = Rs 950, almost double the Rs 500 at 500 m — a small output gain near break-even has a big profit effect.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across all three plants: unit traps, two-step calculations and reading the margins.

questions.q: A spinning mill's monthly fixed cost is Rs 11,400,000, cotton net cost Rs 35 per lb and yarn price Rs 510 per 10 lb. What monthly profit does it earn at 250 bags (100 lb) a day for 30 days?
questions.explain: Daily contribution = 25,000 × 16 = 400,000; monthly = 12,000,000; minus fixed 11,400,000 = Rs 600,000.

questions.q: A student computes the spinning break-even as 380,000 ÷ 16 = 23,750 'bags'. The error is
options: Using the monthly instead of daily fixed cost
The result is lb, not bags — divide by 100 to get 237.5 bags
questions.explain: Contribution is per lb, so 23,750 is the break-even in lb; at 100 lb per bag that is 237.5 bags.

questions.q: The whole weaving shed: 120 looms, daily fixed cost Rs 480,000, contribution Rs 9 per metre. How many metres per day must the shed weave in total to break even? Round to the nearest metre.
questions.explain: 480,000 ÷ 9 = 53,333 m per day, which is 444.4 m × 120 looms.

questions.q: Which plant has the smallest safety margin between actual output and break-even?
questions.explain: Spinning is only 5 % above break-even, weaving about 12.5 % and dyeing 25 %. A 5 % drop in output would wipe out the spinning mill's profit.

questions.q: If the dyeing plant's charges rise by Rs 2 per metre with costs unchanged (contribution Rs 14), what is its new break-even in metres per day with daily fixed cost Rs 480,000? Round to the nearest metre.
In the weaving sheet the daily fixed cost per loom (Rs 4,000) is a variable cost per metre once it is divided by 500 m.
questions.explain: Dividing a fixed cost by output gives a fixed cost per unit that changes with volume; the cost itself is still fixed and does not vary with metres woven.

questions.q: A dyeing plant with daily fixed cost Rs 480,000 and contribution Rs 12 per metre runs at 44,000 m a day. What is its monthly profit over 30 days?
questions.explain: Daily contribution = 528,000; daily profit = 48,000; × 30 = Rs 1,440,000 — equivalently (44,000 − 40,000) × 12 × 30.

questions.q: The spinning mill's depreciation is cut by Rs 600,000 a month after an asset is fully depreciated. Its new break-even in bags per day (30-day month, Rs 1,600 contribution per bag) is
questions.explain: New monthly fixed cost = 10,800,000; daily = 360,000; ÷ 1,600 = 225 bags per day.

questions.q: In the weaving shed, the daily fixed cost per loom of Rs 4,000 was found by dividing by 120 looms. If 20 looms are permanently removed and fixed cost is unchanged, the fixed cost per loom becomes
questions.explain: 480,000 ÷ 100 = Rs 4,800 per loom, so each remaining loom must weave 4,800 ÷ 9 = 533 m to break even — more than its 500 m output.

questions.q: Yarn price Rs 51 per lb, cotton Rs 35 per lb, daily fixed cost Rs 380,000. By how many rupees per lb can the yarn price fall before the mill at 250 bags (25,000 lb) a day stops making a profit? Give two decimals.
questions.explain: Daily profit Rs 20,000 spread over 25,000 lb = Rs 0.80 per lb; at a price of Rs 50.20 the mill exactly breaks even.
